sobre.texto: I’m passionate about technology and chose to make it my profession: today I’m a Software Analysis and Development Technologist with experience in QA, Python automation and SQL reporting, and more than 700 hours of certified training. Before moving into IT, I spent 12 years handling invoicing, inventory, purchase orders and customer service, which gave me discipline, attention to detail and a practical view of how data impacts a business. I enjoy spotting repetitive tasks and turning them into reliable, automated processes, and I’m looking to keep growing in IT by building solutions that make teams more efficient.

qv.b1: Fully restructured a Python + Selenium automation tool that assigns technical tests in Moodle; proposed and built Excel-based batch assignment with automatic Word document generation, cutting the process from 7 minutes to under 30 seconds per candidate.
qv.b2: Built SQL reports consolidating results per candidate (score, level reached, pass rate) for the analytics team.
qv.b3: Ran functional tests and bug reporting, took part in code reviews, wrote technical documentation and administered WordPress and Moodle.

emi.b1: Invoicing, cash handling and customer service on the DOMINIUM POS system; inventory control, purchase orders and supplier relations; administrative support and quality (QMS) and occupational health and safety (OHS) systems.

proyectos.intro: Case studies: the problem, how I solved it, which tools I used and what the result was.

p1.problema: Assigning a technical test to each candidate in Moodle took about 7 minutes of repetitive clicking, and candidates had to be processed one at a time.
p1.solucion: I restructured the tool in Python and Selenium and added a batch mode: it reads candidates from an Excel template and generates one Word document per candidate.
p1.resultado: From 7 minutes to under 30 seconds per candidate, and any number of candidates in a single run.
p1.d1: The original tool automated part of the process, but it was hard to maintain and handled only one candidate per run. I reorganized it by responsibility and validated the input data with Pydantic, so a mistake in the template is caught before touching Moodle.
p1.d2: Batch mode reads the template with openpyxl, assigns the tests in Moodle with Selenium and uses python-docx to generate each candidate's document.
p1.d3: The code belongs to the company, so I don't publish it or show internal screenshots. I can give a demo during an interview.

p2.problema: The analytics team needed each candidate's score, level reached and pass rate, and that data was spread across several Moodle tables.
p2.solucion: SQL queries with JOINs, subqueries and CASE, published as reports inside Moodle (Configurable Reports).
p2.resultado: One consolidated, always up-to-date report, with no spreadsheets built by hand.
p2.d1: Here is an example with generic table names and fictitious data; it shows the structure of the queries without exposing the real database:
p2.d2: The subquery computes the percentage of correct answers for each attempt, and CASE turns the score into a level the team can read at a glance.

p3.problema: A small business needs inventory, invoicing and customers in a single system, with several companies isolated within the same installation.
p3.solucion: An API built with Django and Django REST Framework on PostgreSQL, organized by modules, with business logic in services and everything running in Docker containers.
p3.resultado: 78 automated tests passing with Pytest, including tenant isolation tests.
p3.d1: Personal project in progress. Each module (customers and suppliers, inventory, invoicing) has its own models, services and tests; inventory works as a ledger of movements that are never edited or deleted.
p3.d2: The code is private. I can show and walk through it during an interview.

p4.problema: Copying data from an online book catalog by hand (title, price, rating and availability) is slow and error-prone.
p4.solucion: A Python script with an interactive menu: you pick a category (or all of them), it walks through every page with requests and BeautifulSoup and builds the report with openpyxl.
p4.resultado: A formatted Excel report ready to read: color-coded ratings, auto-sized columns, timestamp and total book count.
p4.d1: It uses Books to Scrape, a public catalog built for practicing web scraping. The code is split in two parts: extraction (scraper.py) and report generation (reporter.py).
p4.d2: The repository is public and includes instructions to run it.

p5.problema: A one-page resume is not enough to show projects and certificates.
p5.solucion: A bilingual static site with no frameworks, dark mode and a filterable certificate gallery.
p5.resultado: Published on GitHub Pages; certificates are published with personal data covered.
p5.d1: Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step. Each language's text lives in JSON files and the gallery is built from a data file.
p5.d2: Before publishing, a Python script covers the ID number and verification codes on every certificate and turns each page into an image, so no hidden text is left underneath.
